source.title: DataShield: Safety-degrading Data Filtering for LLM Benign Instruction Fine-Tuning
source.authors: Jun-Bo Zhang; Qian-Li Zhou; Xin-Yang Deng; Wen Jiang; Jie Pan; Jin-Biao Zhu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses representation measurements to test whether harmfulness perception and response compliance/refusal are distinct processes. It does not apply the original refusal-direction ablation or addition intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper defines a harmfulness-perception direction from prompt activations and a compliance direction from accepted-versus-refused response activations. Results from those measurements and their comparison bear on V5. The data-filtering and fine-tuning benchmark tables do not test the listed direction claims, and the paper does not ablate or add a direction.
record.test_reason: Section III builds a prompt-level harmful-vs-harmless difference-in-means direction and a response-level accept-vs-refuse direction in Llama3-8B-Instruct. It reports their near-orthogonality, 2D projections, and how each shifts under benign fine-tuning. These are correlational representation results bearing on V5 only. There is no ablation, addition or weight edit, and the DataShield filtering and ASR tables test the authors' own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that harm perception and response compliance are independent processes. They find benign fine-tuning leaves harmful-prompt recognition intact but raises overall compliance, which explains the safety loss. The fine-tuning analysis is on Llama3-8B-Instruct, not base Llama3-8B.
record.recipe_differences: The paper measures a prompt-activation harmfulness-perception direction and a response-activation compliance direction, then compares their projections and correlations. It does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction as a causal ablation/addition intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports layer-wise variation: projection scores change more from middle layers onward, and cosine similarities are described across layers. Exact layer-wise numerical values are not provided in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: A response-based compliance projection difference correlates with GPT-4-rated compliance across seven datasets (r > 0.9, p < 0.001) in Llama3, Llama3.1 and Qwen2.5. However, GPT-4 rates instruction adherence, not refusal specifically.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A response-token accept-minus-refuse direction tracks compliance behaviour across datasets and models.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning samples that shift activations furthest along the compliance direction raise ASR the most (e.g. Llama3 Dolly top-1000 DirectHarm4 ASR 91.00 vs 12.75 for the instruct model). The bottom-1000 samples keep ASR near or below the instruct model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection of fine-tuning data on a compliance direction predicts how much benign fine-tuning erodes refusal.

record.problems: The mechanistic findings are primarily qualitative figure-based results without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The mechanistic analysis uses Llama3-8B-Instruct, and there is no causal ablation or addition to establish mediation. The separate fine-tuning projection comparison is also reported for Llama3-8B.
record.rows_left_out: No results were omitted from the listed mechanistic findings. DataShield filtering and safety-benchmark results were not entered as rows because they evaluate sample ranking/filtering rather than the listed direction mechanisms or V5's harmfulness-versus-refusal distinction.

untested.parts: No causal intervention on either direction. Response activations come from teacher-forced canned accept/refuse responses, not the model's own decisions. Only Llama3-8B-Instruct is analysed, with no numeric separation metrics.
The harmless-minus-harmful prompt direction is Arditi's direction up to sign, but it is never ablated or added.
No jailbreak or adversarial-training test of the direction.
Benign fine-tuning shifts compliance, but the study does not test whether training method or timing decides if one removable direction exists.

missing.what: Behavioural refusal loss accompanying the r6 compliance shift. Example: Llama3-8B-Instruct DirectHarm4 ASR rises from 12.75 to 23.75 (Alpaca) or 79.00 (Dolly) after unfiltered fine-tuning. This shows refusal changes while harm perception (r5) does not.
missing.locator: Table III (also Table I Random column)

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'harmfulness perception direction' is the Arditi-style prompt difference-in-means. The finding that it separates prompts by harm regardless of accept/refuse is in line with Zhao et al. on V5, but it is not a V1 test. The compliance direction comes from paired canned responses, so it may partly encode refusal text content rather than the model's decision. Most other results evaluate DataShield's filtering performance and are not rows.

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of a harmful-minus-harmless instruction difference direction; no evaluation of refusal removal or harmless-request over-refusal from such interventions.
No weight-edit ablation or released-model abliteration evaluation.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or of training against its ablation.
The paper distinguishes harmfulness perception from compliance/refusal, but does not test whether refusal itself is affine, conic, or distributed over multiple directions.
The paper measures representational separation and correlations, but does not causally intervene on either process to establish mediation.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the direction.
Benign fine-tuning is examined, but the study does not test whether the timing or method of refusal training determines whether one removable direction exists.

rows.value: Figure only; text says the score trends upward slightly and stays around zero, with scores largely stable in shallow layers and rising from a middle layer.

relationships.condition: Llama3-8B-Instruct, correlational representation analysis, before/after benign LoRA fine-tuning
relationships.reason: Two findings fit separate harm encoding. The harm and compliance directions are near-orthogonal in intermediate layers, and projections sort samples by harm on one axis and by compliance on the other (r1, r4). Under benign fine-tuning, compliance rises a lot while harm perception stays near zero and harmful/benign stay separable (r5, r6, r8). Figure-only evidence with no causal test.
relationships.display_finding: Harm and compliance directions were near-orthogonal and separated their respective classes; benign fine-tuning substantially increased compliance while harm perception stayed near zero and harmful/benign representations remained separable.

labels.label: supports
labels.condition: Llama3-8B-Instruct, correlational representation analysis, before/after benign LoRA fine-tuning
labels.reason: Harm and compliance directions are near-orthogonal in intermediate layers (r1). Projections sort samples by harm on one axis and compliance on the other (r4). After benign fine-tuning, compliance rises a lot, harm perception barely moves, and harmful/benign stay separable (r5, r6, r8). All of it is figure-only and uncontrolled, but it fits V5.

relation.reason: Its own results (Fig. 3a, Fig. 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) bear on whether harm perception is encoded separately from compliance/refusal.

tranche.reason: Section III uses its own correlational method (diff-in-means harm direction, response-level compliance direction, projections, cosines, PCA) to ask whether harm and refusal/compliance are encoded separately. It has no ablation, which is the original's method. The rest of the paper (DataShield) uses the compliance direction as a tool, but Section III reports results bearing on V5.

source_check.notes: The paper calls Llama3-8B-Instruct 'Llama3-8B', and Fig. 4's 'Base Model' is the original instruct model. Section III has no controls and no uncertainty: uncertainty=y comes only from the Fig. 11 r/p values for DataShield's projection proxy. The harm direction is defined as harmless minus harmful, and the authors admit they cannot tell whether the slight score rise means harmful prompts now read as harmless.

statements.correction: arXiv:2606.00160, Llama3-8B-Instruct: the cosine between the harmfulness-perception direction (diff-in-means at the final prompt token) and the compliance direction (mean response activations, accept minus refuse) is close to 0 in intermediate layers. Source is Fig. 3(a) (response-token-averaged hidden states), figure-only. No controls, no uncertainty. Separate author group (Zhang, Zhou et al.).
statements.problem: r1 is cited, but the visible what, conditions and why text never describes this study. The conditions omit its direction types, and the why says 'four author groups', leaving this study out. The visible text gives no numbers for this study.

statements.correction: Cite r5, r6, r8 for this point, not r4. Add that r8 (Fig. 5 PCA) shows benign and harmful samples clearly separable after fine-tuning (figure-only).
statements.problem: The description of this study is right: the harmfulness score rises very slightly and stays around zero, while the compliance score changes much more (Fig. 4, final prompt token, DirectHarm4). Two side issues. r4 is cited, but it is the pre-fine-tuning model with teacher-forced responses, so it does not show harm surviving lost refusal. Section III does not itself state LoRA or the fine-tuning dataset.

reader_labels.reason: The measured directions are near-orthogonal, align differently with refused-harmful and accepted-harmless samples, and harmful/benign representations remain separable; see r1-r8.
